learningObjectives.title: Rate of reaction and collision theory

questions.q: What does the rate of a chemical reaction measure?
options: How much reactant is present at the start
How quickly reactants are converted into products
The total energy released by the reaction
The temperature reached during the reaction
questions.explain: Rate of reaction is a measure of how fast reactants are used up or products are formed over time.

questions.q: According to collision theory, for a reaction to occur particles must collide with sufficient energy and:
options: the correct orientation
the same mass
an equal charge
identical speeds
questions.explain: A successful collision needs both enough energy and the correct orientation of the colliding particles.

questions.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
options: The energy released when products form
The minimum energy particles need to collide successfully and react
The average energy of all the particles
The energy stored in the products
questions.explain: Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles must have for a reaction to take place.

questions.q: In an experiment, 48 cm³ of gas is collected in 24 seconds. What is the mean rate of reaction?
options: 2 cm³/s
0.5 cm³/s
24 cm³/s
72 cm³/s
questions.explain: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 48 cm³ ÷ 24 s = 2 cm³/s.

questions.q: Which method could be used to follow the rate of a reaction that produces a gas?
options: Measuring the volume of gas given off over time
Measuring the colour of the solution only
Weighing the reaction vessel before the reaction only
Recording the room temperature over time
questions.explain: Collecting the gas produced and recording its volume against time lets you track how fast the reaction proceeds.

questions.q: On a graph of gas volume against time, what does a steeper line indicate?
options: A slower rate of reaction
A faster rate of reaction
That the reaction has stopped
That no gas is being produced
questions.explain: A steeper gradient means more product forms per second, so the reaction is faster.

questions.q: Why does the rate of most reactions decrease as the reaction proceeds?
options: The temperature always falls to zero
The reactant concentration falls, so collisions become less frequent
The products speed up the reverse reaction only
The activation energy increases over time
questions.explain: As reactants are used up their concentration drops, reducing the frequency of successful collisions.

questions.q: Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of reaction?
options: Particles gain energy, moving faster and colliding more often with enough energy
Particles become larger and heavier
The activation energy is removed completely
The number of particles doubles
questions.explain: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so collisions are more frequent and more energetic.

questions.q: Why does increasing the concentration of a solution increase the rate of reaction?
options: There are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
The particles move much more slowly
Each particle carries more activation energy
The reaction becomes reversible
questions.explain: A higher concentration packs more reactant particles into the same volume, increasing collision frequency.

questions.q: How does breaking a solid reactant into a powder affect the rate of reaction?
options: It increases the surface area, increasing the rate
It decreases the surface area, decreasing the rate
It has no effect on the rate
It removes the need for activation energy
questions.explain: Powdering a solid exposes more surface area, allowing more frequent collisions and a faster reaction.

questions.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: By providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
By raising the activation energy
By increasing the temperature of the surroundings
By being used up to release energy
questions.explain: A catalyst offers a route with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

questions.q: What happens to a catalyst during a reaction?
options: It is chemically unchanged and not used up
It is completely used up
It becomes a product of the reaction
It turns into a reactant
questions.explain: A catalyst is not consumed, so the same mass remains at the end of the reaction.

questions.q: Increasing the pressure of a reaction between gases increases the rate because:
options: The gas particles are pushed closer together, so they collide more frequently
The particles gain extra activation energy
The gases turn into liquids
The number of gas molecules increases
questions.explain: Higher pressure squeezes gas particles into a smaller volume, increasing collision frequency.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. Which set of conditions would give the fastest reaction?
options: Powdered magnesium with warm, concentrated acid
A single magnesium ribbon with cold, dilute acid
Powdered magnesium with cold, dilute acid
A single magnesium ribbon with warm, dilute acid
questions.explain: Greater surface area, higher temperature and higher concentration all increase collision frequency, giving the fastest rate.

questions.q: Which symbol is used in an equation to show a reversible reaction?
questions.explain: The double half-arrow ⇌ shows that a reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

questions.q: What is meant by a reaction being at dynamic equilibrium?
options: The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
Both reactions have completely stopped
Only the forward reaction is taking place
All reactants have been used up
questions.explain: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue but at equal rates, so amounts stay constant.

questions.q: Equilibrium in a reversible reaction can only be reached in what kind of system?
options: A closed system
An open beaker
A system with no reactants
A system at absolute zero
questions.explain: A closed system stops reactants or products escaping, allowing a balance between the two reactions.

questions.q: Once a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium in a closed system, the concentrations of reactants and products:
options: remain constant
fall steadily to zero
always become equal to each other
keep increasing
questions.explain: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant (though not necessarily equal).

questions.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and turns white. What would adding water to the white solid do?
options: Turn it blue again, showing the reaction is reversible
Keep it white permanently
Turn it black
Cause no change at all
questions.explain: Adding water reverses the change, reforming blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate, demonstrating a reversible reaction.

questions.q: When white ammonium chloride is heated it decomposes, and the white solid reforms on cooling. This shows that the reaction is:
options: reversible
exothermic only
a complete combustion
irreversible
questions.explain: Ammonium chloride breaks down on heating and reforms on cooling, so the reaction goes both ways and is reversible.
